newsitem.title: USA: Du Pont murder trial winding down.
newsitem.headline: Du Pont murder trial winding down.

text.p: Jurors in the John du Pont murder trial were asked in closing arguments on Tuesday to determine if the millionaire chemicals heir knew he was doing wrong in killing Olympic wrestler David Schultz.

Defence attorney Thomas Bergstrom, comparing du Pont's mental state to a waking nightmare, told the 12 jurors evidence presented over 13 days of testimony showed he was driven to kill by delusions caused by long-standing paranoid schizophrenia.

But lead prosecutor Joseph McGettigan said du Pont was driven by anger and resentment rather than legal insanity to kill Schultz and arrogantly believed his wealth and influence would allow him to escape the consequences.

"Anger doesn't mean out of touch with reality," McGettigan said, adding that Schultz was killed "because an arrogant person took the most arrogant act a human being could take." He said du Pont had become increasingly angry with Schultz, who he believed was threatening his position within the wrestling world that du Pont valued highly.

Delaware County Court of Common Pleas Judge Patricia Jenkins was to deliver final instructions to the jury, which was then to be sequestered for deliberations, later in the day. Jurors will be given three counts on which to render a verdict -- first degree murder, third degree murder or voluntary manslaughter.

They can render verdicts of guilty, not guilty, not guilty by reason of insanity, or guilty but mentally ill, which carries the same punishment as a guilty verdict but allows a convicted person to obtain treatment first.

Du Pont, 58, sat passively, as he has throughout the trial, as both lawyers in their closing arguments agreed he was mentally ill and killed Schultz but argued over whether he knew what he was doing was wrong when he shot the wrestler on Jan. 26, 1996.

Failure to know the wrongfulness of one's act is a key criterion for an insanity defence. Bergstrom, arguing for an insanity verdict, said, "You have to look at this evidence through the prism of psychosis. It's not just through a glass darkly -- it's through a shattered glass darkly."

He asked jurors to compare their own brief moments of night-time terrors with what he said was a paranoia and fear that gripped du Pont constantly. This led him to acts such as lining the walls of his house with razor wire and digging up the grounds of his estate looking for the corpse of an imagined chambermaid he believed was his mother.
"Imagine having those nightmares in the light of day ... If you do, I think you'll understand what's in the mind of the defendant," Bergstrom said.

But McGettigan listed actions that he said showed du Pont was aware of the wrongfulness of his act, including taking to Schultz's house a larger gun than he usually carried, firing a third shot into Schultz's prone body, refusing to let police into his home after the killing and repeatedly asking for his lawyer.
"This isn't a person who doesn't know what he's doing. It's a person who knows society's rules," McGettigan said. He said the jury should consider a verdict of guilty but mentally ill.
What was essential, he said in his summation, was that the jury use "the word that holds the murderer responsible ... the word is 'guilty.'"
